analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee and died without a vote or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred sitting members of Congress and their spouses from holding or trading individual stocks, securities futures, commodities, and similar investments while in office, with exceptions for diversified mutual funds, Treasury securities, and qualified blind trusts. Current members would have had 180 days after the law took effect to sell any prohibited holdings. Profits from violations would go to the Treasury, members could face civil fines, and the Government Accountability Office would audit compliance.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want lawmakers making decisions on policy rather than on their personal portfolios. The ban would remove the built-in conflict of interest when a member votes on a bill, regulation, or spending item that could move the price of a stock they or their spouse own. Members themselves also benefit in a sense, by being pushed into blind trusts or diversified funds that can't be influenced by their own official actions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens, by removing conflicts of interest

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits members of Congress and their spouses from holding or trading individual stocks, security futures, commodities, and comparable synthetic investments during the member's term of service, removing the conflict between official duties and personal portfolios.
Requires any profit from a prohibited transaction to be disgorged to the Treasury, bars deducting losses from such transactions, and authorizes civil fines assessed by the ethics committees.
Requires each member to file an annual public certification of compliance and directs the Government Accountability Office to audit members' compliance and report the results.

Allows holdings only in diversified mutual funds or exchange-traded funds, U.S. Treasury securities, or a qualified blind trust, and gives current members 180 days after enactment to sell off prohibited assets.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses, who would have to divest individual stocks and other covered investments within 180 days, give up the ability to pick and trade individual securities while in office, and face fines and profit disgorgement for violations. Some members with large portfolios or a spouse's career in finance would bear the largest adjustment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: The ban restricts even investments members do not control through their official work, and may discourage people of means from serving in Congress or push them to rely on blind trusts that separate them from their family finances.

Enforcement rests with the House and Senate ethics committees themselves, and a member can appeal a fine to a vote of the full chamber, so the people being regulated largely control the enforcement machinery.

The bill does not ban broad index funds or Treasury holdings, and allows compensation from a spouse's primary occupation, so a member whose spouse is a corporate executive or lobbyist would remain untouched by the core restriction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off favors the public: removing the ability of lawmakers to profit from individual stock movements tied to their own votes is a direct answer to a real conflict of interest, and the 180-day divestment window and blind-trust exception soften the burden on members. The design's main weakness is enforcement — the ethics committees and the members themselves would police the rule — and the carve-out for a spouse's outside compensation leaves a notable gap. Still, the costs fall on a small group of sitting lawmakers, not on ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Josh Hawley introduced the bill in the Senate on January 24, 2023.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill received no further action — no committee markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting members of Congress, who keep their ability to hold and trade individual stocks and related investments while in office, with no added penalties, certifications, or audits.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and gave it its only momentum by sponsoring it.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate colleagues
against.what_they_did: No senator signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with a single sponsor and no visible coalition to move it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan breakdown exists — though it drew no support from either side.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their spouses (incumbent officeholders)
industries.note: The bill would force them to divest individual stocks and other covered investments and face fines and profit disgorgement for violations. Their financial interest in keeping the status quo runs directly against the public's interest in conflict-free lawmaking, and with zero cosponsors the bill never advanced.
